biltong.name: Biltong
biltong.summary: An air-dried, cured meat that originated in Southern Africa, made from beef or game meats such as ostrich or kudu, and related to but distinct from beef jerky.

ugali.name: Ugali (pap)
ugali.summary: A stiff cornmeal dish known by many names, including pap and sadza, eaten across many African countries, cooked in boiling water or milk into a firm, dough-like consistency.

clanwilliam-south-africa.name: Clanwilliam
clanwilliam-south-africa.summary: A town in the Olifants River valley in South Africa's Western Cape, about 200 km north of Cape Town, and seat of the Cederberg Local Municipality.

cinsaut.name: Cinsaut
cinsaut.summary: A red wine grape valued for heat tolerance and high yields, important in Languedoc-Roussillon and former French colonies such as Algeria, Lebanon and Morocco.

south-african-wine.name: Wine of Origin
south-african-wine.summary: South Africa's wine designation system, introduced in 1973, defining a hierarchy of production regions, districts and wards with rules on grape origin and vineyard size.

african-cassava-mosaic-virus.name: African cassava mosaic virus
african-cassava-mosaic-virus.summary: A plant virus causing mosaic leaf patterns and chlorosis in cassava, Africa's most-produced food crop, and a major concern in sub-Saharan Africa and the Indian subcontinent.

frank-mcewen.name: Frank McEwen
frank-mcewen.summary: English artist and museum administrator (1907–1994) remembered for promoting Shona artists in Rhodesia and helping found the National Gallery of Zimbabwe.

national-gallery-of-zimbabwe.name: National Gallery of Zimbabwe
national-gallery-of-zimbabwe.summary: Zimbabwe's national art gallery in Harare, opened in 1957 as the National Gallery of Rhodesia, known for showcasing the country's contemporary art including its annual Zimbabwe Heritage exhibition since 1986.

tapfuma-gutsa.name: Tapfuma Gutsa
tapfuma-gutsa.summary: A Zimbabwean stone sculptor born in 1956.

sculpture-of-zimbabwe.name: Shona sculpture
sculpture-of-zimbabwe.summary: An art form, especially stone sculpture, for which Zimbabwe is well known around the world.

kingsley-sambo.name: Kingsley Sambo
kingsley-sambo.summary: A Rhodesian painter and cartoonist who lived from 1936 to 1977.

thomas-mukarobgwa.name: Thomas Mukarobgwa
thomas-mukarobgwa.summary: A Zimbabwean painter and sculptor (1924–1999) who worked as a gallery attendant and became a founding member of Frank McEwen's Workshop School.

joram-mariga.name: Joram Mariga
joram-mariga.summary: Called the "Father of Zimbabwean Sculpture" for his influence on local artists from the 1950s until his death in 2000.

peter-garlake.name: Peter Garlake
peter-garlake.summary: Zimbabwean archaeologist and art historian (1934–2011) known for influential research on Great Zimbabwe and on Ife, Nigeria.

great-zimbabwe.name: Great Zimbabwe
great-zimbabwe.summary: A city in south-eastern Zimbabwe settled around 1000 AD, capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe from the 13th century and the largest stone structure in precolonial Southern Africa, built by ancestors of the Shona people.

rhodesia.name: Rhodesia
rhodesia.summary: An unrecognized state in southern Africa from 1965 to 1979, formed when its white-minority government declared independence from Britain, later becoming Zimbabwe.

edward-paterson.name: Edward Paterson
edward-paterson.summary: Pioneering art teacher (1895–1974) in Rhodesia who founded Cyrene School and introduced the Arts and Crafts style to African students.

berry-bickle.name: Berry Bickle
berry-bickle.summary: Zimbabwean artist born in 1959, based between Zimbabwe and Mozambique, whose work explores the region's history of colonialism; a founding member of Bulawayo's Visual Artists' Association.

ian-smith.name: Ian Smith
ian-smith.summary: Rhodesia's prime minister from 1964 to 1979 (1919–2007), who unilaterally declared independence from Britain in 1965 rather than accept majority rule, leading to sanctions and the Rhodesian Bush War.

robert-mugabe.name: Robert Mugabe
robert-mugabe.summary: Zimbabwean revolutionary and politician (1924-2019) who fought white minority rule, was imprisoned from 1964 to 1974, then led Zimbabwe as prime minister and later president from 1980 to 2017.

joshua-nkomo.name: Joshua Nkomo
joshua-nkomo.summary: Zimbabwean revolutionary and politician (1917–1999) who led ZAPU's guerrilla forces against white minority rule and later served as Zimbabwe's vice-president under Mugabe.

zimbabwe-african-national-liberation-arm.name: ZANLA
zimbabwe-african-national-liberation-arm.summary: The military wing of the Zimbabwe African National Union, which fought against white minority rule in Rhodesia during the Rhodesian Bush War.

zimbabwe-people-s-revolutionary-army.name: ZIPRA
zimbabwe-people-s-revolutionary-army.summary: The military wing of the Zimbabwe African People's Union, formed in the 1960s by Jason Moyo, which fought in the Rhodesian Bush War with Soviet and African Union backing.

angolan-civil-war.name: Angolan Civil War
angolan-civil-war.summary: A civil war in Angola from 1975 to 2002, mainly between the Soviet- and Cuban-backed MPLA and the US- and South Africa-backed UNITA, following independence from Portugal.

mozambican-civil-war.name: Mozambican Civil War
mozambican-civil-war.summary: A civil war fought in Mozambique from 1977 to 1992 between the Marxist FRELIMO government and the anti-communist RENAMO insurgency, killing over a million people amid Cold War rivalries.

south-african-border-war.name: South African Border War
south-african-border-war.summary: A largely asymmetric conflict in Namibia, Zambia and Angola from 1966 to 1990, fought between South African forces and the Namibian independence movement SWAPO's armed wing.

kingdom-of-kongo.name: Kingdom of Kongo
kingdom-of-kongo.summary: A Central African kingdom spanning parts of modern Angola, Congo and Gabon, independent from around 1390 to 1862, later a Portuguese vassal until its monarchy was abolished in 1914.

matabeleland.name: Matabeleland
matabeleland.summary: A region of southwestern Zimbabwe named for its Ndebele ('Amatabele') inhabitants, home to the capital Bulawayo and rich in coal and gold deposits.

gukurahundi.name: Gukurahundi
gukurahundi.summary: Mass killings of Ndebele and Kalanga civilians in Zimbabwe's Matabeleland from 1983 to 1987, carried out by the North Korean-trained Fifth Brigade and widely considered genocide.

rhodesian-african-rifles.name: Rhodesian African Rifles
rhodesian-african-rifles.summary: A regiment of the Rhodesian Army formed in May 1940, recruiting black African soldiers with mostly white officers, and successor to the Rhodesia Native Regiment of World War I.

lancaster-house-agreement.name: Lancaster House Agreement
lancaster-house-agreement.summary: An agreement signed in London on 21 December 1979 that ended the Rhodesian Bush War, restoring British colonial authority for a transition to internationally recognized independence.

zimbabwe-african-national-union.name: ZANU
zimbabwe-african-national-union.summary: A militant socialist organisation that fought white-minority rule in Rhodesia after splitting from ZAPU in 1963; its ZANU–PF wing has governed Zimbabwe since 1980.

5th-brigade-zimbabwe.name: 5th Brigade
5th-brigade-zimbabwe.summary: A Zimbabwean army brigade formed in 1981 and trained by North Korea that carried out the Gukurahundi killings of Ndebele civilians in the 1980s.

rhodesian-armoured-corps.name: Rhodesian Armoured Corps
rhodesian-armoured-corps.summary: The only standing armoured cavalry unit of the Rhodesian Army, nicknamed the 'Black Devils', which fought in World War II and later the Rhodesian Bush War before being replaced in 1980–81.

zanu-pf.name: ZANU–PF
zanu-pf.summary: Zimbabwe's ruling political party since independence in 1980, long led by Robert Mugabe until his removal in a 2017 coup.

tsitsi-dangarembga.name: Tsitsi Dangarembga
tsitsi-dangarembga.summary: Zimbabwean novelist born in 1959 whose 1988 debut, Nervous Conditions, was the first novel in English published by a Black Zimbabwean woman.

nervous-conditions.name: Nervous Conditions
nervous-conditions.summary: A 1988 semi-autobiographical debut novel by Zimbabwean author Tsitsi Dangarembga about a Shona family in 1960s post-colonial Rhodesia, the first English novel by a Black Zimbabwean woman.

doris-lessing.name: Doris Lessing
doris-lessing.summary: British novelist (1919–2013) who won the 2007 Nobel Prize in Literature at 87, the oldest laureate ever; her novels include The Grass Is Singing and The Golden Notebook.

southern-rhodesia.name: Southern Rhodesia
southern-rhodesia.summary: A self-governing British colony in what is now Zimbabwe, run from 1888 by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company and later by a white-minority settler government with discriminatory laws.

shona-language.name: Shona language
shona-language.summary: A Bantu language spoken by over 14 million people in Zimbabwe and Mozambique, encompassing varieties including Zezuru, Manyika, Korekore and Karanga.

solomon-mutswairo.name: Solomon Mutswairo
solomon-mutswairo.summary: Zimbabwean novelist and poet (1924–2005) who wrote Feso, the first novel in the Shona language, and later became a leading figure in the country's literary and cultural institutions.

commonwealth-foundation-prizes.name: Commonwealth Writers' Prize
commonwealth-foundation-prizes.summary: An award from the Commonwealth Foundation, given from 1987 to 2011 for the best book, overall and by region, by writers from Commonwealth countries.

the-grass-is-singing.name: The Grass Is Singing
the-grass-is-singing.summary: 1950 debut novel by British author Doris Lessing, set in 1940s Southern Rhodesia, following a woman's hasty marriage, mental decline and murder amid colonial racial politics.

chirikure-chirikure.name: Chirikure Chirikure
chirikure-chirikure.summary: Zimbabwean poet, songwriter and writer born in 1962, who worked 17 years as a publishing editor and now runs a literary agency.

mbira.name: Mbira
mbira.summary: A family of plucked lamellaphone instruments traditional to Zimbabwe's Shona people, played at religious ceremonies and social gatherings, and added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2020.

national-anthem-of-zimbabwe.name: Simudzai Mureza weZimbabwe
national-anthem-of-zimbabwe.summary: Zimbabwe's national anthem, introduced in 1994 after a nationwide competition to replace a South African-derived song, with Shona lyrics written by Solomon Mutswairo and music by Fred Changundega.

this-mournable-body.name: This Mournable Body
this-mournable-body.summary: A 2018 novel by Tsitsi Dangarembga, the third book in a trilogy following Nervous Conditions and The Book of Not.

the-book-of-not.name: The Book of Not
the-book-of-not.summary: A 2006 semi-autobiographical novel by Zimbabwean author Tsitsi Dangarembga, continuing the story of Tambudzai begun in her earlier novel Nervous Conditions.

michael-joseph-publisher.name: Michael Joseph
michael-joseph-publisher.summary: British publisher and writer, born 1897, died 1958.

jenfan-muswere.name: Jenfan Muswere
jenfan-muswere.summary: A Zimbabwean politician and ZANU–PF member of parliament, appointed Minister of Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services in September 2023 after earlier serving in the communications ministry.

manuel-iii-of-kongo.name: Manuel III of Kongo
manuel-iii-of-kongo.summary: The last Manikongo, or ruler, of the Kingdom of Kongo, reigning as a Portuguese vassal from 1911 to 1914, born Manuel Martins Kiditu in 1872 and dying in 1927.

manikongo.name: Manikongo
manikongo.summary: The title of the ruler of the Kingdom of Kongo (14th–19th centuries), who appointed provincial governors and received tribute, ruling from the capital Mbanza Kongo.

mhondoro.name: Mhondoro
mhondoro.summary: Royal ancestral spirits in Shona traditional religion believed to mediate between God and people; cults centered on them helped organize resistance during Zimbabwe's First and Second Chimurengas.

chimurenga.name: Chimurenga
chimurenga.summary: A Shona word for 'revolutionary struggle,' used for uprisings against British South Africa Company rule in the 1890s and the 1960s-70s war against Rhodesia's white government.

roy-welensky.name: Roy Welensky
roy-welensky.summary: A Northern Rhodesian politician, son of a Lithuanian Jewish father and an Afrikaner mother, who became the second and last Prime Minister of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland from 1956.

federation-of-rhodesia-and-nyasaland.name: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland
federation-of-rhodesia-and-nyasaland.summary: A 1953–1963 colonial federation of Southern Rhodesia, Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland in southern Africa, which collapsed amid growing African opposition to colonial rule.

mwene-muji.name: Mwene Muji
mwene-muji.summary: A polity proposed by historian John Thornton around Lake Mai-Ndombe in the Congo Basin, ruled by the BaNunu, that declined through the 17th to 19th centuries before Belgian conquest.

mushie.name: Mushie
mushie.summary: Town on the Kasai River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, birthplace of the musician Papa Wendo.

rhodesia-s-unilateral-declaration-of-ind.name: Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence
rhodesia-s-unilateral-declaration-of-ind.summary: The 1965 declaration by Rhodesia's white-minority cabinet that the colony was now an independent state, deemed illegal by Britain and the UN, which imposed sanctions in response.

kongo-language.name: Kikongo
kongo-language.summary: A Bantu language of the Kongo people spoken by around seven million people in Central Africa, historically carried across the Atlantic by enslaved Africans.

kituba-language.name: Kituba
kituba-language.summary: A widely used lingua franca in Central Africa, a creole language based on Kikongo, and a national language of the Republic of the Congo and Democratic Republic of the Congo.

kongo-religion.name: Kongo religion
kongo-religion.summary: The traditional animistic beliefs of the Bakongo people, centered on the creator god Nzambi Ampungu and on ancestor veneration.

nzambi-ampungu.name: Nzambi Ampungu
nzambi-ampungu.summary: The Supreme God and eternal Sky Father of traditional Kongo spirituality, associated with the sun; his female counterpart rules the moon. After Portuguese colonization he became identified with the Christian God.

black-consciousness-movement.name: Black Consciousness Movement
black-consciousness-movement.summary: Grassroots anti-apartheid movement that emerged in South Africa in the mid-1960s. It promoted political consciousness and brought greater solidarity among black groups, placing black consciousness at the forefront of the struggle.

pan-africanist-congress-of-azania.name: Pan Africanist Congress
pan-africanist-congress-of-azania.summary: South African pan-Africanist political party founded in 1959 by a group led by Robert Sobukwe that broke from the ANC. It rejected multiracialism and advocated a South Africa based on African nationalism.

sharpeville-massacre.name: Sharpeville massacre
sharpeville-massacre.summary: Shooting on 21 March 1960 in which South African police fired into a crowd of about 5,000 protesting apartheid pass laws. At least 91 people were killed; 21 March is now a public holiday.

ubuntu-philosophy.name: Ubuntu
ubuntu-philosophy.summary: A Bantu African value system emphasizing the interconnectedness of individuals with their society and world, often summarized as 'I am because we are.'

stanlake-j-w-t-samkange.name: Stanlake Samkange
stanlake-j-w-t-samkange.summary: Zimbabwean historian, educator, journalist and author (1922–1988) from an elite nationalist family. He was the most prolific of the first generation of black Zimbabwean writers in English.

steve-biko.name: Steve Biko
steve-biko.summary: South African anti-apartheid activist (1946–1977) and leading figure of the Black Consciousness Movement. Raised in a poor Xhosa family, he began studying medicine in 1966.

national-union-of-south-african-students.name: NUSAS
national-union-of-south-african-students.summary: National Union of South African Students, an influential force in student anti-apartheid politics that moved from liberalism toward radicalism. Its mottos included non-racialism and non-sexism.
national-union-of-south-african-students.source_title: National Union of South African Students

south-african-students-organisation.name: South African Students' Organisation
south-african-students-organisation.summary: Group of black South African university students, formed in 1969, that resisted apartheid non-violently and shaped the Black Consciousness Movement. The government banned it in October 1977.

desmond-tutu.name: Desmond Tutu
desmond-tutu.summary: South African Anglican bishop and anti-apartheid and human rights activist (1931-2021). He was the first black African to serve as Bishop of Johannesburg and as Archbishop of Cape Town.

truth-and-reconciliation-commission-sout.name: Truth and Reconciliation Commission
truth-and-reconciliation-commission-sout.summary: Court-like restorative justice body set up in South Africa in 1996 after apartheid ended. Victims of gross human rights violations gave statements, and perpetrators could testify and request amnesty.

simon-kimbangu.name: Simon Kimbangu
simon-kimbangu.summary: Congolese religious leader (1887–1951) who founded the Christian movement Kimbanguism. His followers consider him an incarnation of the Holy Spirit.

kimbanguism.name: Kimbanguism
kimbanguism.summary: Large African-initiated church, described as para-Christian, with an estimated 6 million believers and headquarters in Nkamba, Kongo Central. It calls itself Jesus Christ's Church on Earth through his special envoy Simon Kimbangu.

world-council-of-churches.name: World Council of Churches
world-council-of-churches.summary: Worldwide Christian inter-church organization founded in 1948 to promote ecumenism. Its members include Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and Baptist churches, and its administrative centre is in Geneva, Switzerland.

john-thornton-historian.name: John Thornton
john-thornton-historian.summary: American historian (born 1949) at Boston University specializing in African, African Diaspora and Atlantic World history.

linda-heywood.name: Linda Heywood
linda-heywood.summary: Caribbean-American historian specializing in African, especially Angolan, history; co-author with her husband John Thornton of award-winning work on Central Africans and the Atlantic world.

saso-bpc-trial.name: SASO Nine
saso-bpc-trial.summary: Nine Black Consciousness activists convicted in South Africa's SASO/BPC trial, held in Pretoria from 1975 to 1976. They were charged with treason and sentenced to five or six years on Robben Island.

aubrey-mokoape.name: Aubrey Mokoape
aubrey-mokoape.summary: South African anti-apartheid activist (1944 to 2020) and leader in the Pan-Africanist Congress and Black Consciousness Movement. First detained at 15, he worked alongside Steve Biko and later became a physician.

mosiuoa-lekota.name: Mosiuoa Lekota
mosiuoa-lekota.summary: South African anti-apartheid activist (1948-2026) who was jailed alongside Nelson Mandela from 1985. He later served as Minister of Defence from 1999 to 2008 and founded the Congress of the People party in 2008.

harvey-sindima.name: Harvey Sindima
harvey-sindima.summary: Malawian theologian, philosopher and professor who wrote on African philosophy and religious ethics. He is the original voice behind umunthu, and teaches at Colgate University.

nganga.name: Nganga
nganga.summary: A spiritual healer, diviner and ritual specialist in traditional Kongo religion, also found among descendants of Kongo and Mbundu peoples across the African diaspora, including Brazil, Cuba and Haiti.

kongo-cosmogram.name: Dikenga (Kongo cosmogram)
kongo-cosmogram.summary: A core symbol of Kongo religion showing the physical and spiritual worlds, the sun's rotation, and the four stages of life, drawn as a cross within a circle.

shona-people.name: Shona people
shona-people.summary: A Bantu ethnic group native to Southern Africa forming the majority in Zimbabwe, who migrated from the Congo River basin around the end of the first millennium and built a great civilization there.

moses-cyrus-weiler.name: Moses Cyrus Weiler
moses-cyrus-weiler.summary: Latvian-born South African rabbi (1907–2000) who founded Reform Judaism in South Africa before moving to Israel in 1958.

simbi.name: Simbi
simbi.summary: A guardian spirit of water and nature in traditional Bakongo religion, also venerated in African diaspora traditions such as Hoodoo and Palo.
